title: Missing values and data-quality checks
objectives: Distinguish missing, non-finite and valid zero values under an explicit field contract.
Produce a quality report that records rejection reasons and reconciles input counts.
Apply missing values and data-quality checks invariants safely and identify scope boundaries.
motivation: A missing value is not automatically zero. A zero-volume observation can be valid while a missing volume means no usable observation was supplied.

blocks.md: A missing value is not automatically zero. A zero-volume observation can be valid while a missing volume means no usable observation was supplied. For a price field this lesson requires a finite, strictly positive float in one stated currency. That policy rejects zero; it does not mean every numeric field or every financial product has the same policy. We use None for a missing scalar and NaN as a non-finite floating representation. NaN is not a reliable equality sentinel: use an explicit missing/finiteness check rather than value == NaN.

blocks.caption: Expected output: [100.0, 102.0], then [(1, 'missing'), (2, 'nonpositive'), (3, 'nonfinite'), (4, 'nonfinite')], then 6. The exact-float contract is deliberate: a production parser may accept other representations, but must declare the conversion before this boundary.

blocks.md: Once parsing has produced a floating NumPy array with missing numeric entries represented as NaN, np.isfinite returns one Boolean per element: False for NaN and either infinity. Finiteness is necessary under our price contract but is not the whole contract: zero and negative finite values still need a separate range check. The symbol & combines array masks elementwise; parentheses around each comparison avoid Python operator-precedence mistakes. np.count_nonzero counts True positions in this Boolean mask.

blocks.code:
import numpy as np
prices = np.array([100.0, np.nan, 0.0, np.inf, 102.0])
valid = np.isfinite(prices) & (prices > 0)
print(valid.tolist())
print(int(np.count_nonzero(valid)))
print(prices[valid].tolist())
blocks.caption: Expected output: [True, False, False, False, True], then 2, then [100.0, 102.0]. A single mask selects data but loses separate rejection reasons unless you record those too. NumPy dependency illustration: not runnable in the app until its runner explicitly supports NumPy. Copy into a prepared local Python environment with NumPy to execute. No installation is required to read or answer this lesson.

blocks.md: Dropping invalid prices changes which observations the calculation describes. The arithmetic mean of observed valid prices is not automatically the mean for the original intended timeline. Report the accepted count, rejected count and time/identity coverage along with the statistic. If every value is rejected, return an explicit no-result state or documented error; do not silently invent a zero mean or divide by zero. This lesson does not claim that deleting missing observations removes statistical bias.

Forward fill carries the last observation into a later missing position. It is a modeling rule, not a fact about the unobserved price. Any use needs a maximum allowed age and explicit handling of identity/session boundaries and corporate actions. Backward fill can import future information into an earlier decision. Do not apply it to a historical trading signal and call that an available-at-the-time observation. The next lesson distinguishes event and availability timestamps; for now, preserve the missing flag and do not invent data.

A useful quality report names schema and field policy, total records, accepted/rejected counts, reason counts, duplicate-key checks and time coverage. Counts should reconcile: accepted plus rejected equals total when every row goes to exactly one branch. Several invalid fields can be tracked per row, but then summed reason counts can exceed rejected row count. State whether reasons are first-error-only or multi-label. Missingness by instrument or session can matter more than one overall percentage.

Independent transfer: implement a validator for synthetic volumes that accepts exact nonnegative integers including zero and excludes bool, None and non-finite values. Report rejected indexes and reasons and reconcile counts. Compare it with the price policy: zero is accepted for volume but rejected for this price interface. Then design an all-invalid input case and state the no-result behavior before computing an average.

Technical reference: [NumPy isfinite](https://numpy.org/doc/stable/reference/generated/numpy.isfinite.html) establishes that NaN and either infinity are non-finite. The exact-float positive-price rule, missing-value policy, report-count examples and availability-time reasoning are lesson specifications and arguments here. They are not rules established by the NumPy copies, broadcasting or isfinite pages.

guidedExercise.prompt: Why can backward filling a missing price invalidate a historical signal test?
hints: Names availability timing as an explicit check.
guidedExercise.solution: It can use an observation not yet available at the signal time. State availability timestamps and model imputation separately from observations.

commonMistakes: A replacement needs a stated source/field contract. Do not transfer a rule for one field to every other field. (The contract must justify the substitution and downstream effect.)
isfinite detects these non-finite cases; it does not enforce a positive-price domain by itself. (These are precisely the non-finite floating cases here.)
Six total records minus two accepted records leaves four rejected records; each rejected record has exactly one first reason in this example.

summary: Missing, invalid, non-finite and zero are distinct states.
Declare policy by field, retain rejection reasons and coverage, and do not confuse imputation with an observation or hide all-invalid results as zero.
Distinguish missing, non-finite and valid zero values under an explicit field contract.

quiz.prompt: A volume field has missing data. When is replacing it with zero justified?
options: Always, because missing and zero are the same number
Whenever it makes the graph look smoother
Only under an explicit field contract
Never for any field under any possible contract
quiz.explanation: A replacement needs a stated source/field contract. Do not transfer a rule for one field to every other field. (The contract must justify the substitution and downstream effect.)

quiz.prompt: Which entries does np.isfinite flag False in a floating array?
quiz.explanation: isfinite detects these non-finite cases; it does not enforce a positive-price domain by itself. (These are precisely the non-finite floating cases here.)

quiz.prompt: Of 6 records in the scalar worked example, 2 are accepted. Under its one-branch-per-record policy, how many are rejected?
quiz.explanation: Six total records minus two accepted records leaves four rejected records; each rejected record has exactly one first reason in this example.

quiz.prompt: Every input price is invalid under the field contract. What should a mean calculation do?
options: Return an explicit no-result/error under its contract
Return zero and label it an observed average
Use the number of rejected rows as the mean
Select a future price without recording it
quiz.explanation: Specify all-invalid behavior before aggregation. Zero can be a real numeric result elsewhere, so it is not a safe unlabelled failure marker. (There are no accepted observations to average.)

quiz.prompt: A report assigns every row to exactly one accepted/rejected branch, but permits several reasons per rejected row. Which statement is correct?
options: Reason counts must always sum to the number of input rows under standard assumptions
Accepted plus rejected equals total; summed reason counts may exceed rejected
Accepted can exceed total when one row has two reasons
Reconciliation is unnecessary because reasons are present
quiz.explanation: Reconcile row counts independently of multi-label reason counts. State the reason policy so the report is interpretable. (The row partition and reason labels are different counts.)
